messages.subject: secr 4.5.8
messages.body_plain:
secr 4.5.8 is on CRAN. New functions (chat.nk, adjustVarD) calculate Fletcher's c-hat and use it to adjust the confidence limits of density estimates for spatial overdispersion*. Several minor bugs are fixed. See here <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/secr%204.5.8%20NEWS.txt> for details.

* These functions are a bit experimental and do not cover all cases.

messages.subject: Sampling across many sites, mask size, and model run time
messages.subject_clean: Sampling across many sites, mask size, and model run time
messages.body_plain:
Hey all,

I've been beating my head against this data set for some time and figure it might be good to just put it out there so that the experts can take a crack.

I'm estimating coyote densities across the state of South Carolina, USA with 8 large (200 - 800 km2) study sites in 2019 and 10 study sites (we added 2 additional sites) in 2020. I've discretized my transects down to 500m apart traps and built a capture history that uses sampling year as my sessions so that I can share parameters across sites (I have very low sample numbers at some sites).

My capture history is summarized as this:

          2019 2020
Occasions     4    5
Detections  104  168
Animals      85  113
Detectors  1326 1592

I've built a mask following the general specifications outlined in the build mask vignette including a buffer that is 4* the larger session's (2020) HN sigma and spacing that is approximately 0.6* the smaller session's (2019) HN sigma.

my_mask <- make.mask(my_traps, buffer = 5500, spacing = 500, type = "trapbuffer")

This gives me what I believe is overkill for buffer and higher resolution for the mask. The problem is that I now have a 2019 mask of 25,681 points and a 2020 mask of 30,463 points and my null model takes 2 hours to run if my computer is feeling up to it. In previous iterations of running this data, I've had more complex models take upwards of 12 hours but I've also observed stark decreases in runtime if I increase my mask spacing to 1000m, 1500m, 2000m, so on and so forth.

So, my question is: at what point do you start tinkering with mask resolution for the sake of reasonable model runs? And, beyond that, is there a better way for me to be doing this? Ultimately I want to use session and sex ID as covariates for detection parameters and then use my best detection model to estimate density by session with basic landcover covariates such as forest cover, etc. Using a significantly reduced mask I've produced satisfactory results, but I want to make sure I'm not biasing my estimates.

Any help to reduce my runtime or general thoughts on my course of action would be much appreciated.

Jordan

messages.subject: Re: Sampling across many sites, mask size, and model run time
messages.subject_clean: Sampling across many sites, mask size, and model run time
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jordan
By all means play with coarser masks, but for safe & convincing (reportable) results you seem to have it about right.

Off the top of my head there are two other options:
1. If the mask areas of different study sites do not overlap (much) then you could treat each year x site as a session and compute sessionxyear-specific masks. Then there are far fewer mask points to be considered for each animal. Year and site effects can be considered through session covariates.
2. You may have a geometry for which the details option 'maxdistance' really helps. Check ?details. I haven't seen this used much in 'secr', but something similar really worked for Turek et al. Ecosphere 2021 (DOI:10.1002/ecs2.338 <http://dx.doi.org/10.1002/ecs2.3385>).

I would be interested to hear the outcome.
Murray

messages.subject: Using SECR for non-camera trap data but for direct sighting data
messages.subject_clean: Using SECR for non-camera trap data but for direct sighting data
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I am a researcher in leopard conservation in South Africa looking at providing population estimates.

I would like to use spatial capture recapture analysis for my data. However, my methodology does not involve camera traps but the collection of direct sightings by professionals guides when on safari.

Here is my first thought:

For the analysis of the direct sighting data, Spatial Capture Recapture method will be adapted as it is normally used for the estimation of population density with camera traps. Each study area will be covered by a grid of 1km2 and the centroid of each grid will be the equivalent of a camera trap location. Each leopard-sighting coordinate recorded will be matched to the coordinate of a grid cell centroid as if the leopard is captured by a camera trap. Is that correct?

SCR requies the following data:

1.      Detectors (is it correct to say the guide is the detector?)

a.      Location (the location of the sighting will be the same as the location of the detector and will not be permanent)

b.      Covariates associated (the covariates should be associated with the guides (i.e. years of experience, hours in the field, km driven) but could the covariates be associated with the location (i.e. distance from a watering hole, habitat type?)

2.      Capture history

a.      Number of leopard encounter by each detector in each sampling occasion (i.e. daily game drive)

b.      Animal level covariates (sex and age)

3.      The survey region

a.      Its location and boundary

b.      Spatial covariates (e.g. distance of sighting from settlement such as lodges, distance from water, habitat types)

If you have other suggestions as to how to analyse direct sighting data, I'd love hear.

Thank you.
Kind regards,
Marine

messages.subject: Re: Using SECR for non-camera trap data but for direct sighting data
messages.subject_clean: Using SECR for non-camera trap data but for direct sighting data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Marine
To use SECR you will need reliable individual identifications - perhaps by matching photos. Is that what you intend? Number of encounters per grid cell is not enough.

Detection covariates will be associated with the detector = grid cell, not with individual guides, and a measure of effort per grid cell will be useful. Other spatial covariates (distance to water, vegetation etc.) must be recorded  for each pixel in the habitat mask (a map of areas containing the activity centres of potentially sighted leopards); they may be useful as covariates of leopard density.

But first check that you really have individual-level capture-recapture data.
Murray

messages.subject: Re: Using DENSITY to estimate the population of the East Balkan distribution of brown bears
messages.subject_clean: Using DENSITY to estimate the population of the East Balkan distribution of brown bears
messages.body_plain:
Hello Haris
Those are fairly big questions. Starting with the easy one: yes, you need cartesian coordinates, and I'm sure QGIS can do that for you - just project to any cartesian system e.g. UTM. Even if you're not used to R, this <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/secr-spatialdata.pdf> may help.

I am guessing that you collected hair samples and identified individuals by DNA? It is important to allow for big differences in search effort, but this is simple enough in the software.

A SECR model fitted to data from a narrow region can certainly be extrapolated to a wider region; whether that 'makes sense' is a matter of biological judgement.
fying.

DENSITY is limited (and certainly doesn't fit open population models). You really should overcome your fear of R! The online interface <https://www.stats.otago.ac.nz/secrapp/> to the R package gets you halfway there, but probably it won't be very satisfying as you really have to grasp how 'secr' works to make the most of it.

Murray
